title: Algebraic and affinoid completed local rings at closed points
statement:
Let $F$ be a complete field with a nontrivial real-valued nonarchimedean absolute value. For $n\ge0$, write $P=F[T_1,\ldots,T_n]$ [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring] and let $J\subseteq P$ be an ideal. Let $F\langle T_1,\ldots,T_nangle$ be the ring of restricted series $\sum_{
u\in\mathbf N^n}a_
u T^
u$, meaning that for every $\epsilon>0$ only finitely many coefficients satisfy $|a_
u|\ge\epsilon$, with Gauss norm $\sup_
u|a_
u|$. Put $B=P/J$ and $C=F\langle Tangle/JF\langle Tangle$, with the quotient seminorm. The ideal $JF\langle Tangle$ is closed, and $C$ is a Noetherian [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring] complete normed $F$-algebra for this quotient norm (the zero algebra is allowed). For every maximal ideal $\mathfrak m\subset C$, its inverse image $\mathfrak p$ under $B	o C$ is maximal, and the induced local map $B_{\mathfrak p}	o C_{\mathfrak m}$ gives an isomorphism $\widehat{B_{\mathfrak p}}\xrightarrow{\sim}\widehat{C_{\mathfrak m}}$ of completions at their respective maximal ideals [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime, def-weil-pbc-adic-completion].

proof.text: Write $D_n=F\langle T_1,\ldots,T_n\rangle$, $D_0=F$. Coefficientwise addition and the finite Cauchy sums give a ring with $\|fg\|\le\|f\|\|g\|$ and the strong triangle inequality. For the product's coefficient decay, bound both coefficient families by $M\ge1$; outside the sum of their finite $\epsilon/M$-exceptional exponent sets, every summand in a coefficient has at least one factor less than $\epsilon/M$. Thus the product is restricted. A Gauss-Cauchy sequence has a coefficientwise limit since $F$ is complete; a uniform approximation by one restricted member shows the limit is restricted and convergence is in Gauss norm. Polynomial truncations are dense. In any $D_n$, $\|h\|<1$ implies $1-h$ is a unit: the partial geometric sums are Cauchy by $\|h^k\|\le\|h\|^k$, and their limit is its two-sided inverse. These arguments also apply to finite tuples with the maximum norm.

source.place: Theorem 3.5.5 Step 3, printed p. 22, supporting analytic comparison; agent reconstruction because the cited PDF is not in this checkout

proof.text: For nonzero $f\in D_n$, $n>0$, divide by a coefficient of maximum absolute value, so $\|f\|=1$. There are finitely many coefficients of norm $1$, and all remaining coefficients have a common bound $\rho<1$: use the finite exceptional set for the threshold $1/2$. Choose positive weights $N_1,\ldots,N_{n-1}$ so that $\nu_n+\sum_{i<n}N_i\nu_i$ takes distinct values on that finite set (successive sufficiently large weights suffice). The substitutions $T_i\mapsto T_i+T_n^{N_i}$ for $i<n$, $T_n\mapsto T_n$, and their minus-sign inverses extend from polynomials by density and completeness; both have operator norm at most $1$, hence are inverse isometries. The unique largest weighted exponent $d$ gives a term $cT_n^d$, $|c|=1$. Every other contribution of norm $1$ has $T_n$-degree less than $d$, so the coefficient $a_d$ is $c$ plus terms of norm at most $\rho$, and all coefficients above $d$ have norm at most $\rho$. The geometric-series argument makes $a_d$ a unit of $D_{n-1}$ with it and its inverse of norm $1$. Multiplying the transformed $f$ by $a_d^{-1}$ gives precisely a series to which the cited division/preparation theorem applies. It follows that the transformed principal ideal $(f)$ contains a monic $w\in D_{n-1}[T_n]$ with lower coefficient norms at most $1$, and division by $w$ has quotient and remainder norm at most the dividend's norm.

source.place: Theorem 3.5.5 Step 3, printed p. 22, supporting analytic comparison; agent reconstruction because the cited PDF is not in this checkout

proof.text: We prove by induction on $n$ that every submodule $M\subseteq D_n^r$, for every finite $r$, has generators $v_1,\ldots,v_t$ and a constant $K>0$ such that every $v\in M$ can be written $v=\sum b_jv_j$ with $\max_j\|b_j\|\le K\|v\|$. Empty generators handle the zero submodule. At $n=0$, choose an $F$-basis of $M\subseteq F^r$. Row reduction gives a nonsingular square minor; its inverse expresses the basis coefficients as finite linear combinations of coordinates, bounding them by a fixed constant times the maximum coordinate norm. This proves the initial case, including $r=0$. For the inductive step assume the assertion in dimension $n-1$ for all finite ranks; the following two steps establish it in dimension $n$.

source.place: Theorem 3.5.5 Step 3, printed p. 22, supporting analytic comparison; agent reconstruction because the cited PDF is not in this checkout

proof.text: First let $I\subseteq D_n$ be a nonzero ideal. Choose a nonzero element and apply step 2; since the coordinate maps are isometries, it suffices to work in the new coordinates, where $w\in I$ is monic of degree $d$ as there. If $d=0$, $I=D_n$ and $1$ is a bounded generator. Otherwise put $A=D_{n-1}$. The remainders of members of $I$ on division by $w$ form exactly $M=I\cap A[T_n]_{<d}\subseteq A^d$: subtraction of a multiple of $w\in I$ stays in $I$, and the remainder of a polynomial of degree less than $d$ is itself by uniqueness. The dimension-$n-1$ induction supplies generators $r_j$ of this submodule with controlled coefficients. For $h\in I$, division gives $h=qw+r(h)$ with $\|q\|,\|r(h)\|\le\|h\|$, and then $r(h)=\sum a_jr_j$, $\max\|a_j\|\le K\|h\|$. Thus $w,r_j$ are the required bounded generators of $I$. Transporting them back by the inverse isometry proves the assertion for the original ideal.

source.place: Theorem 3.5.5 Step 3, printed p. 22, supporting analytic comparison; agent reconstruction because the cited PDF is not in this checkout

proof.text: For submodules of $D_n^r$, now induct on $r$, the case $r=0$ being zero. Project $M$ to the last coordinate, an ideal $I$. Use step 4's bounded ideal generators $g_j$ and choose fixed lifts $v_j\in M$ of them. For $v\in M$, express its last coordinate as $\sum b_jg_j$ with $\max\|b_j\|\le K_I\|v\|$. The vector $z=v-\sum b_jv_j$ has last coordinate zero and $\|z\|\le\max(1,K_I\max_j\|v_j\|)\|v\|$. The rank-$r-1$ induction applied to the kernel submodule expresses $z$ in fixed generators with the corresponding fixed bound. Together with the $v_j$ these generate $M$ with a uniform bound. If $I=0$, apply the kernel argument directly. This completes both inductions; no closedness hypothesis was used.

source.place: Theorem 3.5.5 Step 3, printed p. 22, supporting analytic comparison; agent reconstruction because the cited PDF is not in this checkout

proof.text: Every ideal $I$ of $D_n$ is therefore finitely generated, which is exactly Noetherianity [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring]. It is also closed. For $x\in\overline I$ choose $y_k\in I$ with $\|y_k-x\|\le2^{-k}$. Set $z_0=y_0$ and $z_{k+1}=y_{k+1}-y_k$; then $\|z_{k+1}\|\le2^{-k}$. Express each $z_k$ in the fixed bounded generators $g_j$ from the induction, with coefficients $b_{jk}$ satisfying $\|b_{jk}\|\le K\|z_k\|$. For every $j$, the partial sums of $b_{jk}$ are Cauchy in $D_n$ by the strong triangle inequality, so converge to $b_j$. Finite distributivity and continuity of multiplication give $x=\sum_jb_jg_j\in I$. This proves closedness for every ideal, in particular $JD_n$. Ideals of $D_n/JD_n$ are images of their inverse-image ideals in $D_n$; images of finite generating sets generate, so $C$ is Noetherian as well.

source.place: Theorem 3.5.5 Step 3, printed p. 22, supporting analytic comparison; agent reconstruction because the cited PDF is not in this checkout

proof.text: The quotient seminorm of $D_n/I$ is a norm for any proper closed ideal $I$: norm zero means a representative lies in $\overline I=I$. Taking infima over representatives gives scalar homogeneity, the strong triangle inequality and submultiplicativity. Also $\|1\|\le1$; positivity and $\|1\|\le\|1\|^2$ give $\|1\|=1$. Thus the scalar map is isometric when the quotient is nonzero. It is complete. For a Cauchy sequence of cosets choose a subsequence $c_k$ with successive differences of quotient norm less than $2^{-k-2}$. Lift each difference to $h_k\in D_n$ of norm less than $2^{-k-1}$; this follows from the definition as an infimum, not from attainment of the infimum. Lifting $c_0$, the sums of these $h_k$ converge in $D_n$, and their image is the limit of this subsequence, hence of the original Cauchy sequence. This applies to $I=JD_n$; if $I=D_n$, the quotient is the complete zero ring allowed in the statement. Scalar compatibility and submultiplicativity make it the asserted complete normed $F$-algebra.

proof.text:
For later use prove by induction on $n$ that $D_n/N$ is finite over $F$ for every maximal ideal $N$. For $n=0$ it is $F$. For $n>0$, $D_n$ is not a field: $T_n
e0$ and evaluation at all variables zero shows $T_n$ is not a unit. Hence $N
e0$. Step 2 supplies, after its $F$-algebra coordinate change, a monic $w\in N$ of degree $d>0$. Division shows $D_n/(w)$ is free of rank $d$ over $A=D_{n-1}$, with basis $1,T_n,\ldots,T_n^{d-1}$; existence gives spanning, uniqueness gives independence. Thus the field $L=D_n/N$ is a finite $A$-module. Put $D=\operatorname{image}(A	o L)$; $L$ is finite and therefore integral over $D$ by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-algebra-is-integral]. For $0
e b\in D$, a monic relation for $b^{-1}\in L$, multiplied by $b^{e-1}$, expresses $b^{-1}$ as an element of $D$. Thus $D$ is a field, so $\ker(A	o L)$ is maximal. The dimension-$n-1$ induction makes $D/F$ finite, and finite spanning sets for $L/D$ and $D/F$ multiply to a finite spanning set for $L/F$. The coordinate change fixes $F$, so this proves the claim for the original $N$.

proof.text: Fix now a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ of $C$, and let $N\subset D_n$ be its inverse image; it is maximal and contains $JD_n$. Step 8 makes $L=D_n/N$ a finite-dimensional field over $F$. Steps 6 and 7 supply its quotient vector-space norm $\nu$ without assuming it is multiplicative. For the image $a_i$ of $T_i$ one has $\nu(a_i^k)\le\|T_i^k\|=1$ for every $k\ge0$. Apply [lem-trf-finite-extension-bounded-powers-polynomial] to obtain monic $q_i(T_i)\in F[T_i]$ of positive degree with coefficients of norm at most $1$ and $q_i(a_i)=0$. Thus $q_i(T_i)\in N\cap P$. This includes $a_i=0$ and inseparable algebraic coordinates.

source.place: Theorem 3.5.5 Step 3, printed p. 22, supporting analytic comparison; agent reconstruction because the cited PDF is not in this checkout

proof.text: For $k\ge1$ put $Q_k=(q_1(T_1)^k,\ldots,q_n(T_n)^k)\subset P$. Each $q_i^k$ remains monic with coefficient norms at most $1$. Divide successively by these polynomials using [lem-trf-tate-weierstrass-norm-division], viewing all other variables as coefficients. The result $R_k(h)$ has degree less than $k\deg(q_i)$ in each variable, hence is a polynomial in the finite rectangular monomial span. Each division remainder operator is linear and norm nonincreasing. For a polynomial, canceling its highest term by a multiple of the monic divisor strictly decreases degree, so terminates and produces the same unique remainder. On each polynomial monomial, a remainder operator acts only on its own variable power. Thus the separate-variable operators commute on polynomials, kill multiples of the corresponding $q_i^k$, and fix the rectangular span. Density and continuity give these identities on $D_n$. The successive division identities show $h-R_k(h)\in Q_kD_n$, while $R_k$ kills $Q_kD_n$. Therefore its kernel is exactly $Q_kD_n$. Restriction to $P$ is ordinary multivariable remainder, with kernel $Q_k$. It follows that the inclusion induces the specific isomorphism $P/Q_k\xrightarrow{\sim}D_n/Q_kD_n$, with both sides represented uniquely in that same rectangular span. For $n=0$ the empty rectangle is the constants and $Q_k=0$.

source.place: Theorem 3.5.5 Step 3, printed p. 22, supporting analytic comparison; agent reconstruction because the cited PDF is not in this checkout

proof.text: Put $\mathfrak p_0=N\cap P$. Since $Q_1\subseteq\mathfrak p_0$, step 10 for $k=1$ identifies the ideal $N/Q_1D_n$ with its inverse-image ideal $\mathfrak p_0/Q_1$ in $P/Q_1$. Hence $P/\mathfrak p_0\to D_n/N$ is an isomorphism and $N=\mathfrak p_0D_n$: the preimage of $N/Q_1D_n$ is generated by $\mathfrak p_0$ because the quotient map from $P$ is surjective. In particular $\mathfrak p_0$ is maximal. Because $J\subseteq\mathfrak p_0$, its image $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak p_0/J$ is the required maximal inverse image in $B$. For every $k\ge1$, $Q_k\subseteq\mathfrak p_0^k$. Quotienting step 10's isomorphism further by the ideal generated by $\mathfrak p_0^k+J$ gives $P/(\mathfrak p_0^k+J)\xrightarrow{\sim}D_n/(N^k+JD_n)$, since extension of an ideal commutes directly with finite sums and products of its generators. Equivalently the actual ring map induces $B/\mathfrak p^k\xrightarrow{\sim}C/\mathfrak m^k$.

source.place: Theorem 3.5.5 Step 3, printed p. 22, supporting analytic comparison; agent reconstruction because the cited PDF is not in this checkout

proof.text: For a ring $R$ and maximal ideal $\mathfrak a$, every element $s\notin\mathfrak a$ is invertible modulo $\mathfrak a^k$: choose $t$ with $st=1-v$, $v\in\mathfrak a$, and use $t(1+v+\cdots+v^{k-1})$ as its inverse modulo $\mathfrak a^k$. Fractions [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime] therefore identify $R/\mathfrak a^k$ with $R_{\mathfrak a}/(\mathfrak aR_{\mathfrak a})^k$; the inverse sends $r/s$ to the displayed inverse of $s$ times $r$, and the fraction relation ensures it is well defined. Apply this for $B,\mathfrak p$ and $C,\mathfrak m$ to step 11. All maps come from $B\to C$, so they commute with reduction from $k+1$ to $k$. Taking compatible sequences, as in [def-weil-pbc-adic-completion], gives an isomorphism of the two completions; its inverse applies the inverse finite-level isomorphisms componentwise, which are compatible by uniqueness of inverse. Thus it is precisely the map induced by the local homomorphism in the statement. If $C=0$ there is no maximal ideal and this last assertion is vacuous.
